title: Using the mind for extreme performance

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Over the past century, science has played an integral part in improving sports performance. This began with German physiologist August Krogh's pioneering work on respiration and circulation, which contributed hugely to the development of exercise physiology. Danish exercise physiologist, Erik Hohwü Christensen continued this in the late 1930s with his study of carbohydrate and fat metabolism, which laid the foundation for sports nutrition. Since then, science has contributed to knowing what to eat and drink before, during and after exertion, and how to refine the finer points of technique. In swimming, that goes all the way down to the arrangement of one's fingers to get the most out of every stroke. It has contributed to the evolution of better sporting equipment and clothes, such as the suits elite swimmers use in order to reduce water resistance.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: However, in terms of optimising mental performance, sports science still has a long way to go, especially in a sport where the difference between winning and losing is measured in milliseconds. John Bertrand, a champion Australian yachtsman and sports mentor, says athletes utilise a mere 9-10% of the potential of the human brain. He says that if this potential were maximised, it would be a breakthrough. Elite-level sports psychology does not advance via lab tests; instead the real science is happening out in the field, in the pool or on the track, often by trial and error. It is simply one-on-one training between athletes and coaches, often drawing on life lessons learned elsewhere. Bertrand is tapping into traditional 'mindfulness' techniques and pushing the boundaries to discover the secrets of people who excel in unrelated fields, such as how the SAS commandos train for missions and how ballet dancers maintain their focus.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Andy Walshe of Southern Cross University, Australia, is a specialist in optimising human performance. His technique is grounded in the rite-of-passage rituals of very old cultures, where young people face challenges designed to induce self-reflection and understanding. 'It's a very old tool to which we are applying cutting-edge technology, to understand more completely what actually happens,' he says. His methods involve putting people in unfamiliar, stressful situations. At the opening reception for a conference at which he was presenting, participants wore masks and were prohibited from talking about themselves. What this little exercise reveals is that the precise situation does not matter: what counts is that people are pushed far enough out of their normal comfort zones. To take another example, public speaking is many people's greatest fear, so Walshe might ask a client to perform stand-up comedy or improvise. The key is for the challenge to be scary but not so terrifying that one totally freezes up. There are more intense programs. In 2013, Walshe took Australian ironman champion Matt Poole and three other elite athletes on a nine-day mountaineering expedition in Chilean Patagonia. There, they leaped across glacial crevasses, climbed treacherously unstable slopes and camped in a snowstorm to ultimately summit a never-before-climbed Andean peak. Poole echoes Bertrand's belief that the great undiscovered territory for athletes remains the mind.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Mackenzie Havey, a US-based running coach and author of Mindful Running, believes that athletes focus too much on things that should be automatic. He says that cognitive resources can go into worrying about the task rather than performing it, and the goal is for athletes to learn to do what they have spent years training themselves to do, without too much self-scrutiny. Pre-race nerves are connected with the amygdala, a part of the brain which controls responses to moods. However, Havey cautions that deliberately trying to suppress negative thoughts is counterproductive because the very process of trying to force an idea out often invites it in. The aim is simply to recognise these thoughts for what they are and not dwell on them, instead of attempting to push them aside as though they don't exist.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: John Bertrand recalls talking to the Australian Olympic running champion Cathy Freeman. She told him about coming out of the starting blocks perfectly, about being in harmony with her running as she entered the back straight, and about feeling no pain as she ran to the finish line. 'She did not talk to me once about winning the medal, Bertrand says. 'She talked about the wonderment of the process. This is a fundamental aspect to performing at your best, Bertrand says, 'where you are freeing the mind from the consequences of winning or losing'. Freeman's attitude epitomises the idea of 'do', not 'try', in which the details became the focus of her race.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Jeff Simons, a professor of sports psychology at California State University, USA, recalls a story about Steve Moneghetti, the marathon runner from Australia who was one of the great marathoners of his time but had never earned a medal in a world championship until 1997 in Greece. He did not run well in the qualifiers in this championship and, as the final drew near, it became clear that the high temperature would make it a difficult race. Worse still, he was suffering from a bruised Achilles tendon. Everything seemed against him. Despite this, he qualified for the final. At first, he was left behind by the lead pack, so he decided to aim for a top-20 finish, and got into his rhythm. He persevered, came third, and went on to compete in four Olympic Games. There is no doubt that psychology is what delivers the advantage in competitions, and if elite athletes are able to maximise their mental capacities, performance in sport could be greatly improved.
